newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says Thailand mulls Natuna gas pipeline.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says Thailand mulls Natuna gas pipeline.

text.p: Indonesia's state oil company Pertamina said on Wednesday the Petroleum Authority of Thailand (PTT) had promised to study the feasibility of a pipeline between Thailand and the giant Natuna offshore gas field.

"Pertamina and PTT agreed on August 21 in Bangkok to discuss further a natural gas pipeline from Natuna. We will have another meeting, possibly at the end of this month in Indonesia, at which PTT is expected to give a response," Yaved Sumbung, Pertamina's chief of liquefied natural gas, told reporters.
"Pertamina has said it can't compete with countries near Thailand, such as Myanmar (Burma) or Malaysia, on gas prices," he added.
"What we can offer from Natuna is security of long-term gas supply. PTT has indicated it needs around 960 million standard cubic feet a day of gas," Sumbung added.
Natuna is more than 1,200 km (750 miles) from Bangkok but a new line could conceivably be tied into existing pipelines in the Gulf of Thailand.
Sumbung said Pertamina has also offered Natuna gas to Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.
Indonesia signed an agreement in late 1994 with U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp to exploit the Natuna field in the South China Sea.
The field contains an estimated 210 trillion cubic feet (Tcf) of gas, of which 45 Tcf are thought to be recoverable commercially. Development is projected to cost some US40 billion.
Pertamina, the world's largest supplier of liquefied natural gas (LNG), owns 24 percent of the Natuna project but has been discussing the sale of some of its stake to Japanese companies.
Exxon has a 50 percent interest in the project and Mobil Corp 26 percent.
Gas from the field is expected to start flowing by 2003/2004, offsetting a natural decline from Indonesia's ageing Arun LNG project in northern Sumatra.
